title: Lab 502 - Docker Volumes, Bind Mounts and Port Mapping

lab_objective.description: By performing this lab, you will learn:
objectives: Understand why persistent storage is required in Docker.
Understand what happens to container data when a container is removed.
Understand the difference between Docker volumes and bind mounts.
Create and manage Docker volumes using docker volume commands.
Inspect Docker volumes using docker volume inspect.
Mount Docker volumes into containers using the -v option.
Understand how data is shared between Docker volumes and containers.
Verify data persistence after stopping and removing containers.
Reuse an existing Docker volume with another container.
Create bind mounts using directories from the Docker host.
Mount host directories into containers using the -v option.
Understand the difference between source and destination paths in a bind mount.
Create and modify files on the Docker host and access them inside containers.
Verify that changes made inside a container are reflected on the Docker host.
Understand the difference between read-write and read-only bind mounts.
Publish container ports to host ports using the -p option.
Understand host-to-container port mapping.
Run multiple web server containers simultaneously using different host ports.
Verify web applications using curl and a web browser.
Inspect container mount configurations using docker inspect.
scenario: You are a Linux administrator responsible for deploying containerized web applications using Docker. Your organization requires application data to remain available even when containers are stopped, restarted, or removed.

Your first assignment is to create a Docker volume named webdata and mount it inside an Apache container named volume-httpd. You must create a directory named /linoop and a file named docker.txt inside the mounted volume.

You must verify that the data remains available after stopping and removing the Apache container. You must then create another container named volume-httpd2 and reuse the same Docker volume to verify data persistence.
Your second assignment is to create a bind mount using a host directory named /root/webdata. You must mount this directory inside an Nginx container named bind-nginx at /usr/share/nginx/html.
You must create an index.html file on the Docker host with the specified content and verify that the Nginx container can access and serve the file.
You must also modify the HTML file from inside the container and verify that the changes are reflected in the original file on the Docker host.

Your third assignment is to create another Nginx container named readonly-nginx using the same host directory as a read-only bind mount. You must verify that files can be viewed but cannot be modified from inside the container.
Finally, you must deploy the containers using different published host ports and verify that the web applications are accessible through their respective ports.

tasks.title: Create and Inspect a Docker Volume
steps: Verify the available Docker volumes using the docker volume ls command.
Create a Docker volume named webdata using docker volume create.
Verify that the webdata volume has been created successfully.
Inspect the webdata volume using docker volume inspect.
Identify the Mountpoint of the volume on the Docker host.
Understand that Docker manages the volume storage location.
Display the available Docker volumes again and verify webdata.

tasks.title: Mount a Docker Volume Inside an Apache Container
steps: Pull the httpd:latest image from Docker Hub if it is not already available.
Create and run a container named volume-httpd using the httpd:latest image.
Run the container in detached mode using the -d option.
Mount the webdata Docker volume inside the container at /usr/local/apache2/htdocs using the -v option.
Publish host port 8087 to container port 80 using the -p option.
Verify that the volume-httpd container is running.
Verify the published port mapping using docker ps.
Access the running Apache container using docker exec.
Create a directory named linoop inside the mounted volume.
Navigate to the /usr/local/apache2/htdocs/linoop directory.
Create a file named docker.txt.
Add the following exact content to docker.txt:
Welcome to LINOOP! Learning Docker volumes and persistent storage.
Display the contents of docker.txt.
Verify that the file exists inside the mounted volume.
Exit the container shell.
Verify the container's mount configuration using docker inspect.
Identify the volume name, source, and destination paths.

tasks.title: Verify Volume Persistence After Container Removal
steps: Verify that volume-httpd is running.
Stop the volume-httpd container using docker stop.
Verify that the container has stopped.
Remove the volume-httpd container using docker rm.
Verify that the container has been removed.
Verify that the webdata volume still exists using docker volume ls.
Inspect the webdata volume using docker volume inspect.
Create and run another Apache container named volume-httpd2.
Mount the existing webdata volume inside the new container at /usr/local/apache2/htdocs.
Publish host port 8088 to container port 80.
Verify that volume-httpd2 is running.
Access the container using docker exec.
Navigate to /usr/local/apache2/htdocs/linoop.
Verify that docker.txt still exists.
Display the contents of docker.txt and verify the exact required content.
Verify the web page using curl http://localhost:8088/linoop/docker.txt.
Confirm that Docker volume data remains available even after the original container is removed.

tasks.title: Create and Configure a Bind Mount
steps: Create a directory named /root/webdata on the Docker host.
Verify that the directory exists on the Docker host.
Create a file named index.html inside /root/webdata.
Add the following exact content to index.html:
Hello from LINOOP! This page is served using a Docker bind mount.
Save the file on the Docker host.
Verify the contents of /root/webdata/index.html.
Pull the nginx:latest image from Docker Hub if it is not already available.
Create and run a container named bind-nginx using the nginx:latest image.
Run the container in detached mode using the -d option.
Mount the host directory /root/webdata inside the container at /usr/share/nginx/html using the -v option.
Publish host port 8089 to container port 80.
Verify that the bind-nginx container is running.
Verify the published port mapping using docker ps.
Access the container using docker exec.
Verify that /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html exists inside the container.
Display and verify the exact contents of index.html inside the container.
Verify the bind mount configuration using docker inspect.
Identify the host source directory and container destination directory.

tasks.title: Verify Two-Way Data Sharing Through a Bind Mount
steps: Display the contents of /root/webdata/index.html on the Docker host.
Access the bind-nginx container using docker exec.
Navigate to /usr/share/nginx/html.
Modify index.html from inside the container.
Add the following exact content to the existing file:
Updated from inside the Docker container!
Display the updated contents of index.html inside the container.
Exit the container shell.
Display /root/webdata/index.html on the Docker host.
Verify that the new content is also available on the Docker host.
Modify index.html directly on the Docker host.
Add the following exact content:
Updated from the Docker host!
Access the Nginx web page using curl http://localhost:8089.
Verify that the latest content is displayed.
Confirm that changes made on either side are reflected on the other side because both locations reference the same files.

tasks.title: Create a Read-Only Bind Mount
steps: Create and run another Nginx container named readonly-nginx.
Run the container in detached mode using the -d option.
Mount the existing host directory /root/webdata inside the container at /usr/share/nginx/html.
Configure the bind mount as read-only using the :ro option.
Publish host port 8090 to container port 80.
Verify that readonly-nginx is running.
Access the container using docker exec.
Navigate to /usr/share/nginx/html.
Verify that index.html exists and display its contents.
Attempt to create a file named test.txt inside /usr/share/nginx/html.
Verify that the file creation fails because the bind mount is read-only.
Attempt to modify index.html from inside the container.
Verify that the modification is denied.
Exit the container shell.
Verify that the original index.html on the Docker host remains unchanged.
Access the Nginx web page using curl http://localhost:8090.
Confirm that the read-only bind mount allows the container to read files but prevents it from modifying the mounted host directory.

tasks.title: Final Container, Volume, Bind Mount and Port Mapping Verification
steps: Verify that volume-httpd2 is running.
Verify that bind-nginx is running.
Verify that readonly-nginx is running.
Confirm that all three containers are running simultaneously.
Verify that volume-httpd2 publishes host port 8088 to container port 80.
Verify that bind-nginx publishes host port 8089 to container port 80.
Verify that readonly-nginx publishes host port 8090 to container port 80.
Verify the volume-httpd2 mount configuration using docker inspect.
Verify the bind-nginx mount configuration using docker inspect.
Verify the readonly-nginx mount configuration using docker inspect.
Verify that webdata is a Docker-managed volume.
Verify that /root/webdata is being used as a bind mount.
Verify that the bind-nginx mount is read-write.
Verify that the readonly-nginx mount is read-only.
Display all running containers using docker ps.
Verify Apache access using curl http://localhost:8088/linoop/docker.txt.
Verify Nginx access using curl http://localhost:8089.
Verify read-only Nginx access using curl http://localhost:8090.
Access the Apache and Nginx web applications through a web browser using the Docker host IP address and their respective published ports.
Confirm that all applications are accessible through their respective host ports.

completion_message: Lab 502 completed successfully! You have created and managed Docker volumes, mounted persistent storage inside containers, verified data persistence after container removal, configured bind mounts, practiced two-way data sharing between the Docker host and containers, configured read-only bind mounts, inspected mount configurations, and published container ports to access multiple web applications simultaneously.
